explanations.answer: The house of the LORD in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah, king of Judah, sends word and letters inviting everyone to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:1). One address, no confusion. I wish my own directions were that clear. "Follow the smell of cookies" only gets a baker so far.
Bethel never comes up in this passage. The invitation names one place only: the house of the LORD in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:1). A good invite names the place, friend.

Shiloh isn't named anywhere in this passage. Hezekiah, Judah's king, invites them to keep the Passover at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:1). That's the whole destination. Nobody needs a map and a prayer to find it.

explanations.answer: Keep it in the second month
explanations.explanation: The king, his officials and the whole assembly in Jerusalem decide to keep the Passover in the second month (2 Chronicles 30:2). They missed the regular time, so they pick a new one. I think that's the right kind of stubborn. They don't skip it, they just reschedule it. I've rescheduled plenty of batches myself, friend, and the cookies still came out fine.

That's not the plan in the text. The king, his officials and the whole assembly decide to keep it in the second month (2 Chronicles 30:2). They don't sit around waiting for next year. They pick a date and go.

explanations.answer: Keep it in their own towns
explanations.explanation: The text sends everyone toward Jerusalem. The decision is to keep the Passover in the second month, and the proclamation says the people should come to keep it in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:2, 5). So the call is to come to Jerusalem, not to keep it in their own towns.

explanations.answer: Too few priests were consecrated and the people weren't gathered
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: not enough priests had consecrated themselves, and the people hadn't been gathered in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:3). Two things weren't ready, so the regular time passed. Think of a bakery trying to open with half the staff still tying aprons. The doors just can't open yet.

explanations.answer: The temple was still locked and its lamps were out
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about a locked temple or lamps. It gives two reasons: not enough priests had consecrated themselves, and the people hadn't been gathered in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:3). The problem was people not being ready.

explanations.answer: The king was at war and the roads were closed
explanations.explanation: War and closed roads never show up here. The text says not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people hadn't been gathered in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:3). I know a war makes a tidy excuse, friend, but the text doesn't give it.

The text says, “This plan pleased the king and the whole assembly.” (2 Chronicles 30:4) Everybody's on board, from the king down. That's rare, friend. I can't even get a room to agree on which cookie shape goes first.

The text says the opposite: “This plan pleased the king and the whole assembly.” (2 Chronicles 30:4) King and assembly together are pleased with the new date. That's the verse, friend, and it's a good start.

That's right. The letter says, “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to those of you who remain…” (2 Chronicles 30:6). It's an invitation to come back, with a promise attached. Most mail I get is a bill, friend, so I'd read this one twice.

The letter does say it. It reads, “Children of Israel, return to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that He may return to those of you who remain…” (2 Chronicles 30:6). The call is to return to the LORD, so that He may return to those who remain. It's a warm line, even though the letter gets honest right after it.

The letter says, “Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever.” (2 Chronicles 30:8) Instead of stiff necks, they're called to bow low and come to the place God set apart. Stiff necks and baking don't mix, friend. Ask my mustache about the first week I tried to bend over a rolling pin.

The letter doesn't mention the wilderness. It says, “Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever.” (2 Chronicles 30:8) The call points toward the sanctuary, the place He consecrated.

A camp isn't where the letter points. It says, “Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary, which He has consecrated forever.” (2 Chronicles 30:8) The word is sanctuary, a place God has set apart. That's where the letter wants them headed.

Not quite. The letter says the opposite: “For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and sons will receive mercy in the presence of their captors and will return to this land.” (2 Chronicles 30:9) Their captured family can come home. I know a little about being stuck somewhere dark, friend, and a line like that hits me right in the apron.

The letter holds out hope. It says, “For if you return to the LORD, your brothers and sons will receive mercy in the presence of their captors and will return to this land.” (2 Chronicles 30:9) Mercy for the captured ones and a way home. That's a good reason to turn around.
The letter gives the reason itself: “For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful…” (2 Chronicles 30:9). They can count on Him because of who He is. Nothing else needs to be on the list, friend.

explanations.answer: He owes their fathers a debt
explanations.explanation: The letter never says anything like that. Its reason is “For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful…” (2 Chronicles 30:9). It points to who He is, not to a debt.

The letter doesn't say that either. The reason it gives is “For the LORD your God is gracious and merciful…” (2 Chronicles 30:9). The promise is that He will not turn His face away if they return to Him, and the reason is who He is.

That's what happens. The couriers travel from city to city through Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, “…but the people scorned and mocked them.” (2 Chronicles 30:10) A king's invitation, and that's the reply. I think that one stings, friend.

explanations.answer: They welcome them in every city
explanations.explanation: No, the text says the people scorned and mocked the couriers (2 Chronicles 30:10). A few did respond, though, because some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came (2 Chronicles 30:11). So the text reports mockery, and it also reports some who came.

explanations.answer: They arrest them at the gates
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any arrests. It says the people scorned and mocked the couriers (2 Chronicles 30:10). Mockery is bad enough without adding handcuffs to the story.

The text says, “Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 30:11) The mockers didn't get the last word. Some people heard that invitation and came, and I love that for them, friend.

The text says it plainly: “Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 30:11) Even after the scorn, some came. That's a bright spot after the mockery, friend.

explanations.answer: One heart to obey the king's command
explanations.explanation: The text says the power of God was on the people in Judah “…to give them one heart to obey the command of the king and his officials according to the word of the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 30:12) One heart, and it comes with the power of God. I've watched six cookie cutters argue over one counter, so I know that's no small gift.

Assyria isn't the topic of this verse. The power of God gives the people of Judah one heart to obey the command of the king and his officials according to the word of the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:12). The gift is unity in obeying, and the text doesn't mention a battle.

explanations.answer: Gold to fill the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Gold isn't in this verse. The power of God is on the people of Judah to give them one heart to obey the command of the king and his officials according to the word of the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:12). It's a gift of the heart, and it can't be counted in a treasury.

explanations.answer: The altars and the incense altars
explanations.explanation: The text says they proceeded to remove the altars in Jerusalem and take away the incense altars (2 Chronicles 30:14). They're clearing the city before the Passover. I clean my bakery before guests arrive too. The difference is I only sweep up crumbs.

explanations.answer: The money changers and their tables
explanations.explanation: Money changers don't show up in this passage. The crowd removes the altars in Jerusalem and takes away the incense altars (2 Chronicles 30:14). The cleanup here is all about altars.

explanations.answer: The golden calves and their shrines
explanations.explanation: Golden calves and shrines aren't mentioned here. The text says the crowd removed the altars in Jerusalem and took away the incense altars (2 Chronicles 30:14). Easy one to mix up, friend, but the verse sticks to altars and incense altars.

explanations.answer: Throw them into the Kidron Valley
explanations.explanation: The text says they took away the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 30:14). That's a full clear-out. They didn't just push them to the side. I once swept a whole batch of burnt crumbs behind the oven, friend, and this crowd would not approve.

explanations.answer: Set them up outside the city
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. They threw them into the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 30:14). Nothing about setting them up again anywhere.

explanations.answer: Hand them over to the priests
explanations.explanation: No handoff to the priests is mentioned. The text says they removed the altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 30:14). The crowd did this cleanup themselves.

The text says, “The priests and Levites were ashamed, and they consecrated themselves…” (2 Chronicles 30:15). Then they got moving and did something about it. I think it takes a humble heart to stand there and say, okay, let's fix this. That's good baking and good living, friend.
The text gives a different feeling. The priests and Levites were ashamed, and they consecrated themselves (2 Chronicles 30:15). Proud isn't the word the text uses, friend.
The text names another feeling. The priests and Levites were ashamed, and they consecrated themselves (2 Chronicles 30:15). The word is ashamed, friend, not angry.

That's the opposite of what the text says. A large number of the people, many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, had not purified themselves, “…yet they ate the Passover, contrary to what was written.” (2 Chronicles 30:18) So those people did eat, and the text says plainly it was contrary to what was written.

The text says these people did not sit out. Many from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun had not purified themselves, “…yet they ate the Passover, contrary to what was written.” (2 Chronicles 30:18) They came to the table without being cleansed first. That's why the next verse matters so much.

explanations.answer: He speaks up for them before the LORD
explanations.explanation: The text says Hezekiah interceded for them (2 Chronicles 30:18). He stood in the gap and prayed. I think a king who prays for the crowd instead of scolding them is worth following, friend.

explanations.answer: He sends them away from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That isn't what Hezekiah does. The text says he interceded for them (2 Chronicles 30:18). Nobody is shown the door in this passage, and he prays for them instead.

explanations.answer: He bars them from the temple
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Hezekiah interceded for them (2 Chronicles 30:18). He's not locking doors, and he's praying for the very people who came in.

explanations.answer: Sets his heart on seeking God
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah prays for “…everyone who sets his heart on seeking God…” (2 Chronicles 30:18-19). The heart is what he lifts up in the prayer. Seeking God is the thing he names, and I think that's a very good thing to be known for.

explanations.answer: Brings the biggest offering to God
explanations.explanation: That isn't in Hezekiah's prayer. He asks for atonement for everyone who sets his heart on seeking God (2 Chronicles 30:19). It's about a seeking heart and has nothing to do with whose offering is biggest.

explanations.answer: Was born in the land of Judah
explanations.explanation: Birthplace isn't part of the prayer. Hezekiah asks for atonement for everyone who sets his heart on seeking God (2 Chronicles 30:19). Just before the prayer, the text says many of the people who hadn't purified themselves were from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun (2 Chronicles 30:18).
The text says, “And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.” (2 Chronicles 30:20) Hezekiah prayed, and the LORD answered. I love how short that verse is, friend. It doesn't need a speech.
The text says the opposite: “And the LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.” (2 Chronicles 30:20) The prayer was heard and the people were healed. Short verse, big mercy.

The text says Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who performed skillfully before the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:22). A king noticing good work and saying so. I'd cry happy tears if somebody did that after my first pan of cookies, friend.

The text doesn't mention land. It says Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who performed skillfully before the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:22). Land would've been a nice gift, friend, but the verse names encouragement.
Nothing about promotions in this verse. Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites who performed skillfully before the LORD (2 Chronicles 30:22). He lifts them up with his words.

explanations.answer: Keep the feast seven more days
explanations.explanation: The text says, “The whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days…” (2 Chronicles 30:23). Seven days of joy, then seven more. I've seen a party fade the minute the cookies run out, friend. They kept this one going for seven more days.

explanations.answer: Head home the very next morning
explanations.explanation: That isn't what happens. The text says, “The whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days…” (2 Chronicles 30:23). The agreement is to observe seven more days, friend.

explanations.answer: Hold the feast again next year
explanations.explanation: Next year isn't in the text. It says, “The whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days…” (2 Chronicles 30:23). The agreement is for seven more days, not another feast next year.

The text says the opposite. The whole assembly of Judah rejoiced along with the priests and Levites and the whole assembly that had come from Israel, including the foreigners who had come from Israel and those who lived in Judah (2 Chronicles 30:25). The foreigners are named among those who rejoiced. So leaving them out doesn't match the text.

The text names a wide crowd. The whole assembly of Judah rejoiced along with the priests, the Levites, the assembly from Israel, and the foreigners who came from Israel and those who lived in Judah (2 Chronicles 30:25). Everybody's invited into the joy. I'd want a crowd like that in my bakery.

The text says nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon, David's son and king of Israel (2 Chronicles 30:26). That's a big comparison, friend. The verse points all the way back to Solomon's days.

Absalom, another of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:3), isn't the name in this verse. The text says nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David king of Israel (2 Chronicles 30:26). Solomon's days are the ones it points back to.

Adonijah, another of David's sons (2 Samuel 3:4), isn't who the verse names. The text says nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David king of Israel (2 Chronicles 30:26). It's Solomon's days it remembers.

explanations.answer: It reaches God's holy dwelling in heaven
explanations.explanation: The text says the priests and Levites stood to bless the people, and God heard their voice, “…and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven.” (2 Chronicles 30:27) They blessed, God heard, and the prayer came into heaven. That's the whole answer, friend, and it's worth a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: The king has it written in his records
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says God heard their voice, and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven (2 Chronicles 30:27). It goes to heaven, no filing cabinet involved.

explanations.answer: The people repeat it all through the night
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a night of repeating is in the text. It says God heard their voice, and their prayer came into His holy dwelling place in heaven (2 Chronicles 30:27). The prayer goes up to heaven, and that's where the verse ends.
